name: Eastern Tamang
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Eastern Tamang is not in the catalog. The single sweep hit (Glottolog 48056, Pittman 1971 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies') is the same paper as Pittman 1970 in Hale & Pike, Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal Part II pp. 1-8, already held on file (chep1245; copy placed under east2347). Glottolog attached it to taj by 'computerized assignment from \"tamang\"'; the paper's Tamang data are Taylor's Sahugaon material (Western Tamang, tdg) and its 'stressed/unstressed' terms label four tone/register classes of monosyllables, so it is about a different variety and silent on word-stress placement (priority none). The sweep then pulled the open Mazaudon corpus from HAL (2005 proceedings paper, 2014 LD&C article, 2007 French encyclopedia entry, 2008 Phonetica, 1993 orthography paper) plus the held Owen-Smith 2015 SOAS thesis (Indrawati Khola, Sindhupalchok). The best first-hand statement is Mazaudon 2014: 599-600 (with Mazaudon 2005: 10), Risiangku Eastern Tamang: an initial-stress-plus-tone analysis was considered and rejected; suffixes are not weaker in intensity; 'all syllables are evenly stressed'; prosody is four word tones on the phonological word. Reading: no word stress (word-tone language). Unread but potentially relevant: Mazaudon 1973 Phonologie tamang (SELAF, print-only; pp. 61-92 is where the rejection is demonstrated), Poudel 2006 Dhankute Tamang grammar (HathiTrust search-only, Harvard print) and Lee 2011 Eastern Tamang Grammar Sketch (not located) - medium priority as possible modern grammar-based stress remarks. Everything fetched sources is with.duckduckgo unreachable, OpenAlex and Google Books APIs HTTP 429; HAL needs a non-Mozilla user readers (Anubis challenge). Four small files in the east2347 folder  were written there at 10:19 by something other than this readers and were not opened or listed.

new_statements.quote: [p. 599] But I soon discovered that changing the suffix on a verb root or on a noun did not change the melody of the word. Grammatical morphemes did not have a tonal specification of their own. Nor were they pronounced with a fixed F0 pattern, as a neutral tone might be, or with less intensity. So an interpretation of the system as a combination of an initial stress with four tones, which would all be neutralized in suffixes, although considered for a moment, was rejected (Mazaudon 1973b:61-91). [p. 600] These are also different from the Tamang type, where all syllables are evenly stressed.
new_statements.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 2014. Studying emergent tone-systems in Nepal: Pitch, phonation and word-tone in Tamang. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 587-612 (Risiangku dialect, Sindhupalchok; Eastern Tamang [taj]). Open access: http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24617; HAL halshs-01118386.
new_statements.locator: pp. 599-600 (§5 'Word-tone' and §6 'Some brief typological considerations'); HAL PDF pages 14-15
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tamang is a word-tone language: one of four lexical melodies (tone 1-4, distinguished by pitch, phonation and initial voicing) is attached to the root and spread over the entire phonological word (root + suffixes/clitics). There is no culminative word stress: all syllables of the word are evenly stressed, grammatical suffixes are not reduced in intensity, and Mazaudon explicitly rejected an 'initial stress + tone' analysis. Corroborated by Mazaudon 2005 (HAL preprint p. 10): 'Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed'; Bodish languages 'do not generally give prominence, either by way of F0 or intensity, to one syllable per unit'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress at any level within the word per the source).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Tamang. The 2005 paper contrasts Lhasa Tibetan, where inflectional suffixes are de-stressed and tonally extrametrical, with Tamang where they are not. Mazaudon 2007 (encyclopedia preprint) calls grammatical morphemes 'enclitiques et atones', i.e. toneless, not stressless. Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970: 116 claim first-syllable word stress, but for Western Tamang (Sahugaon, Nuwakot), a different language (west2415).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical root plus case/TAM suffixes and enclitics) is the tone domain; the 'first (tonic) syllable' of the word determines the melody (Owen-Smith 2015: 66, citing Mazaudon 1973 ch. 3), but this is tone assignment, not stress. Statements are about connected speech and framed elicitation of Risiangku Tamang.
new_statements.identity_note: All Mazaudon material describes the Risiangku dialect (Sindhupalchok District, east of the Trisuli), which Gao & Mazaudon 2022 (p. 2) label 'Risiangku Tamang, an Eastern Tamang variety (ISO [taj])' = east2347; Owen-Smith 2015 (Indrawati Khola, Sindhupalchok) is the same language. The one source that states a positional stress rule ('always on the first syllable'), Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970: 116, describes the Sahugaon dialect of Nuwakot and calls it 'Western Tamang' = Glottolog west2415 (ISO tdg), a different language; Pittman 1970's 'three-tone, two-stress' remark rests on the same Western data. The held file named mazaudon_2003_tamang_thurgood-lapolla_chapter.* is actually the 2007 French encyclopedia preprint (HAL halshs-00147443), not the Routledge chapter.

Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 587-612 (Risiangku dialect of Eastern Tamang, fn. 1 p. 587); corroborated by Mazaudon 2005, On tone in Tamang and neighbouring languages, HAL preprint p. 10: 'Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed.'
new_statements.locator: pp. 599-600 (HAL PDF pp. 14-15; text lines 640-648 and 709)
new_statements.reading: Eastern Tamang (Risiangku) has no word stress: an initial-stress-plus-tone analysis was explicitly tested and rejected in the primary 1973 phonology, suffix syllables are not weaker in intensity, and all syllables of the word are evenly stressed; prosody is a four-way word-tone contrast anchored on the root and spread over the whole phonological word. If the language is added to the catalog it should be coded as 'no word stress / tone language', not fixed-initial.

sources.note: p. 599: grammatical suffixes are not pronounced with less intensity, so an analysis as 'initial stress + four tones neutralized in suffixes' was rejected (citing Mazaudon 1973b: 61-91); p. 600: 'the Tamang type, where all syllables are evenly stressed'. Tone (4 melodies) is a property of the whole phonological word.

sources.quote: Each phonological word carries one tone, which is determined by the first syllable (the 'tonic syllable'), and is realised across all the syllables of the word (for a detailed account see Mazaudon 1973: chapter 3). Therefore, within the phonological word heterotonic sequences are not attested. The post-tonic syllables of the word have more phonological and phonotactic restrictions than the tonic syllable: they cannot contain long vowels, and can only contain restricted set of consonant clusters.
sources.locator: sec. 3.1.1, pp. 66-67 (text lines 3317-3331); p. 374 prosody not investigated
sources.note: Secondary phonology sketch following Mazaudon 1973 for a Sindhupalchok (Eastern-area) dialect: word tone set by the first ('tonic') syllable, post-tonic syllables phonotactically reduced. 'Tonic' here means tone-bearing root syllable, not a stress statement; the author says prosody was not investigated. Silent on stress placement.

sources.quote: Le tamang de l'Est, et particulièrement celui du bourg de Risiangku qui sert de référence pour cette présentation, a conservé presque intacte la structure phonologique qu'on peut reconstruire pour l'ensemble de la branche. [...] Les quatre tons du tamang, numérotés de haut en bas de 1 à 4 dans la transcription, sont lexicalement attachés au lexème radical et portent phonologiquement sur le mot entier. Les morphèmes grammaticaux sont enclitiques et atones. [English: Eastern Tamang, particularly that of the village of Risiangku, which serves as reference here, has kept almost intact the phonological structure reconstructible for the whole branch. ... The four Tamang tones, numbered 1-4 from high to low, are lexically attached to the root lexeme and phonologically span the whole word. Grammatical morphemes are enclitic and toneless/unaccented.]
sources.note: Describes Eastern Tamang prosody as four word tones anchored on the root with unaccented ('atones') enclitic grammatical morphemes; no explicit statement about stress position. Consistent with the 2005/2014 'no word stress' reading.

sources.quote: At the same time, I worked out the tonal system of a dialect of Eastern Tamang, which, unsurprisingly, had similar characteristics. The demonstration was done in my dissertation in 1971 and was published in 1973. (Mazaudon M., 1973b:61-92). [...] There is a typological difference, however, between Lhasa Tibetan and languages of the Tamang group. Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed. In Lhasa Tibetan, inflectional (as opposed to derivational) suffixes, like case-markers and verbal suffixes, are de-stressed.
